title: Generative Forecasting from Coarse-Grained Observations: When Does Cascading Help?

paper.title: Generative Forecasting from Coarse-Grained Observations: When Does Cascading Help?
paper.abstract: Abstract We study probabilistic forecasting of dynamical systems such as fluids and waves from coarse observations. Since the unseen fine scales influence the dynamics, the same coarse initial state can evolve into a whole distribution of futures. Generative forecasters may produce visually plausible samples, but it is hard to tell whether they sample the right conditional distribution, since trajectory data contain a single future for each initial state. We address this problem by generating reference data in a hierarchical way: for each coarse initial state, we generate many different fine-scale components and numerically evolve the full states. Using these conditional ensembles, we show that standard diffusion models and stochastic interpolants make substantial distributional errors. We then show that cascading shorter forecasts greatly reduces these errors for the turbulent flows and waves we study, but we also find and characterize cases in which it hurts. Since the coarse process is not Markov, cascading discards information about the unresolved fine scales even with exact transitions. To understand this, we propose a solvable analytic model which shows that the optimal cascade depth decreases as the coupling between the unresolved and observed scales gets stronger, and increases as the dependence of the forecast on the observation becomes more oscillatory. Consistent with our experiments, cascading is detrimental when the direct forecast is “easy” to learn, for example Gaussian as in the passive scalar case. We release our datasets as a first benchmark for probabilistic forecasting with ground-truth conditional ensembles.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Suppose we observe a turbulent flow on a coarse grid and want to predict what it will look like some time later. The grid resolves the large scales, but the unobserved fine (subgrid) scales also influence the dynamics. In 1969, Lorenz argued that in a flow with many scales, a fine-scale error propagates to ever larger ones. Two states that differ only in smallest details become as different as two random states, in finite time ( Lorenz, 1969 ; Palmer et al., 2014 ) . Weather forecasting is a classic example of this “butterfly effect” ( Lorenz, 1963 ) . The same coarse observation X 0 X_{0} is therefore consistent with many futures X T X_{T} , one for each subgrid realization, and the forecast is the conditional distribution P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}) ( Chorin et al., 2000 ; Chorin et al., 2002 ) . A modern approach is to learn P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}) with conditional generative models such as diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021 ) and stochastic interpolants (SIs) ( Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ) 1 1 1 A more detailed discussion is in Appendix A . trained on pairs of initial and final observed states. These models generate samples of future weather and turbulent flows ( Price et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Kohl et al., 2026 ) which resemble real physical states, but do they actually sample from the right conditional distribution ( Theis et al., 2016 ) ? Testing this is a challenging problem. One reason is that the conditional distribution describes all futures consistent with a given observation but available data usually only contain one trajectory per initial state. Here we address this challenge. We design an experiment that lets us show that common generative forecasters can make substantial distributional mistakes. We then study a way to reduce these mistakes by better using the available data: forecasting over shorter time intervals and composing the results. Practical forecasters already do this, but mostly as a matter of convenience. Our goal is to understand when and why it helps, and when it can actually hurt. The experiment works as follows. For five spatio–temporal systems with different dynamical characteristics we first generate coarse states and then complete each coarse state with many independently drawn fine-scale components (Section 2 ). The full states are identical under coarse graining, but the dynamics (computed by a numerical solver) evolve them into different coarse futures. For each coarse initial state this yields a reference ensemble from the conditional distribution, whose statistical properties can be studied empirically. We test a standard conditional SI and a conditional diffusion model trained directly on initial–final pairs ( X 0 , X T ) (X_{0},X_{T}) , and find that they can be substantially wrong. Figure 2 shows an example for Euler flow (second and third rows). Their samples have visually correct local statistics, but the global structure is completely wrong. Diffusion models and SIs generate samples via stochastic dynamics in an auxiliary “diffusion” time. This dynamics is in general very different from the physical dynamics of the system over the forecasting period. A forecaster trained only on pairs ( X 0 , X T ) (X_{0},X_{T}) has to learn in one fell swoop everything the physical dynamics does between 0 0 and T T . But the physical dynamics is a composition of many short steps. As intermediate observations at times 0 < t < T 0<t<T are often available ( Rühling Cachay et al., 2023 ; Rozet and Louppe, 2023 ) , it is natural to ask whether they can be leveraged to improve conditional forecasting. Instead of learning P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}) directly, one can learn the conditional transitions P ⁡ ( X t i + 1 ∣ X t i ) P(X_{t_{i+1}}\mid X_{t_{i}}) over S S shorter intervals and compose them into a cascade of depth S S . In a cascade of SIs, the generative path is then forced to agree with the physical evolution at some intermediate times. In the Euler example, such a cascaded SI approach is much better than direct and it effectively reproduces the conditional distribution (last row of Figure 2 ). In practice, the depth of a cascade is set by a fixed time step: GenCast rolls out a twelve-hour transition over fifteen days ( Price et al., 2025 ) , and conditional diffusion models and SIs for fluid simulation use the time step of the training data ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Kohl et al., 2026 ; Mücke and Sanderse, 2026 ) . Cascading can, however, also discard information even with exact transitions. Only the full state evolves by composing short steps. After coarse graining, the unresolved fine scales carry information from one interval to the next, so that the coarse process is not Markov. To our knowledge, there is no analysis of how cascading affects the learned distribution. The questions we ask here are: is it better to forecast directly or with a cascade, what properties of the physical system determine the answer, and how deep should a cascade be? We propose a solvable model to answer these questions (Section 3 ). The optimal cascade depth results from the interplay between easier learning and memory loss, and depends on the specific system under study. If the conditional distribution is easy to learn over the full horizon, cascading can be detrimental. This is the case for a scalar field passively advected by a steady flow, whose conditional distribution stays Gaussian at every horizon, with a mean affine in the observation and a covariance that does not depend on it (Section 5 ). Our main contributions are the following. • An experimental design that enables proper evaluation of the conditional distribution. New datasets for five physical systems, with different simulated futures for each observed initial state, allow us to compare learned and true conditional distributions on every observation (Sections 2 and 4 ). To our knowledge, these are the first datasets designed for this notoriously challenging problem; we release them as an openly accessible benchmark. We find that diffusion models and SIs trained directly over the forecast horizon sample substantially wrong conditional distributions in four of the five systems, despite producing visually plausible samples. • A theoretical explanation. For smooth dynamics, we show that, through nonlinear interactions, the conditional mean leaves a fixed approximation class as the horizon grows, and that, under partial observation, a fine cascade of exact transitions loses the conditional spread of the forecast. We construct a stylized model of a rotating system driven by a hidden Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process where we compute the error of a simple SI exactly and prove that it is minimized at a finite depth S ⋆ ≥ 2 S^{\star}\geq 2 ; with the rotation switched off, every cascade is worse than the exact direct forecast (Section 3 ). • An experimental test. At a fixed number of supervised transitions, cascading reduces the error of the direct forecasters by factors between 2.3 2.3 and 5.7 5.7 , with the smallest error at an intermediate depth, for nonlinear flows and linear waves alike. For the passive scalar, every added stage increases the error, consistent with the analysis (Section 5 ).

sections.text: We consider a physical system whose full state Y t Y_{t} evolves according to Y t = 𝒢 t ​ ( Y 0 ) Y_{t}=\mathcal{G}_{t}(Y_{0}) . A forecaster sees only the coarse state X t = ℋ ⁡ ( Y t ) X_{t}=\mathcal{H}(Y_{t}) . At the initial time, we write Y 0 = ( X 0 , Z 0 ) Y_{0}=(X_{0},Z_{0}) , where Z 0 Z_{0} contains the fine-scale components. Since the observation X 0 = x 0 X_{0}=x_{0} generally does not determine Z 0 Z_{0} , different full initial states consistent with the same observation can lead to different observed futures. The forecasting task is therefore to learn the conditional distribution P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0}) (2.1) for every observation x 0 x_{0} . In our systems, Y t Y_{t} consists of one or two fields on a two-dimensional periodic domain, simulated on grids ranging from 128 2 128^{2} to 1024 2 1024^{2} points. The observation map ℋ \mathcal{H} keeps only their Fourier modes with 0 < | k | ≤ 8 0<|k|\leq 8 (196 real coordinates per field), while the unresolved initial modes extend to higher wavenumbers that depend on the system (Appendix B.1 ).

sections.heading: Why trajectory data are not enough.
sections.text: A generative forecaster learns an approximation P ^ ​ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) \widehat{P}(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0}) from which it can draw samples. To measure its accuracy, we would like to compare the learned and the true conditional distributions for each observation, using some metric D D on probability distributions, and then average over observations, ℰ ⁡ ( P ^ ) = 𝔼 x 0 ∼ P ⁡ ( X 0 ) ​ [ D ⁡ ( P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) , P ^ ​ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) ) ] . \mathcal{E}(\widehat{P})=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}\sim P(X_{0})}\Bigl[D\bigl(P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0}),\,\widehat{P}(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0})\bigr)\Bigr]. (2.2) Estimating ℰ \mathcal{E} requires many samples from P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0}) for each of many observations x 0 x_{0} . But data usually contain only one future per observed initial state, with all observed states being different. Proper scoring rules can rank forecasters on such data ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) , but they cannot determine how far they are from the true conditional. Averaging final spectra or other statistics over initial conditions only tests the marginal distribution P ⁡ ( X T ) P(X_{T}) . Comparing the joint distributions of ( X 0 , X T ) (X_{0},X_{T}) could in principle work because they determine the conditionals. The issue is that a forecaster that generates the “correct” forecast for a slightly perturbed observation would have a nearly correct joint distribution, but the forecasts could be completely wrong if they are sensitive to the initial state (which is often the interesting regime).

sections.heading: Direct forecasters can sample the wrong distribution.
sections.text: Using our reference ensembles, we can check whether a learned forecaster samples the right conditional distribution. This leads to our first major finding. Figure 2 shows results for a two-dimensional Euler flow, where the forecaster observes a coarse-grained initial vorticity. We trained two strong generative forecasters on pairs ( X 0 , X T ) (X_{0},X_{T}) from the training ensembles: a conditional SI ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , which we call Direct SI, and a conditional elucidated diffusion model (EDM) ( Karras et al., 2022 ) . We then drew 10,000 10{,}000 samples from each model for a held-out observation. We find that both models generate plausible individual samples. However, a closer look reveals that the large-scale structure of their forecasts is wrong. Indeed, the reference mean has a distinct large-scale geometry, and the reference standard deviation is strongly heterogeneous, while the means of the two forecasters are “washed out”, and their standard deviations are nearly uniform. The same happens for waves in heterogeneous media (Appendix B.5 ). Figure 2: Direct forecasters can sample the wrong conditional distribution. One held-out Euler observation (top left). Each row shows three samples of the vorticity at time T T , followed by the conditional mean and the pointwise standard deviation over 10,000 10{,}000 samples. Reference: the simulator, run from 10,000 10{,}000 fine-scale completions of the observation. Direct SI and EDM: generative forecasters trained on pairs ( X 0 , X T ) (X_{0},X_{T}) . Cascaded SI: the cascaded forecaster of Section 3 at the validation-selected depth S ⋆ = 10 S^{\star}=10 , discussed in Section 5 .

In practice, however, the transitions are learned from finite data with a model of finite capacity, which is why shorter transitions can help. We analyze the two effects in turn and then show how they trade off.

sections.heading: Why can shorter transitions be easier to learn?
sections.text: Over a long horizon, the future observation can depend on the initial one in a nonlinear or oscillatory way, which a model of finite capacity may not be able to represent. Over a short horizon this dependence may be simpler. We make this precise for the conditional mean m t ​ ( x ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ X t ∣ X 0 = x ] m_{t}(x)=\mathbb{E}[X_{t}\mid X_{0}=x] , since an error in the conditional mean implies an error in the distribution (Proposition C.7 ). We model limited capacity by a fixed class ℱ \mathcal{F} of functions of the observation, such as the polynomials of a given degree. For smooth dynamics, the distance from m t m_{t} to ℱ \mathcal{F} grows like c n ​ t n / n ! c_{n}t^{n}/n! for short horizons, where t n t^{n} is the first power in the expansion of m t m_{t} whose coefficient lies outside ℱ \mathcal{F} (Theorem C.1 ). For quadratic dynamics, such as Galerkin truncations of the Euler equations, and quadratic ℱ \mathcal{F} , this coefficient is cubic in the observation and appears at order t 2 t^{2} (Theorem C.2 ). Repeated nonlinear interactions then create a dependence that a quadratic map cannot represent. It can however be represented by a composition of short maps from the same class. When the full state is observed, composing S S fitted polynomial maps of a fixed degree over intervals of length δ = T / S \delta=T/S converges to the true map over [ 0 , T ] [0,T] as δ → 0 \delta\to 0 , whereas a single fitted polynomial keeps a positive error (Theorem C.5 ).

sections.heading: Why can too many short transitions hurt?
sections.text: Even when the short transitions are exact, they can incur a memory loss. Along a true physical trajectory, the fine scales at time t i t_{i} are shaped by the unobserved initial state and by the evolution up to t i t_{i} , and they continue to act on the coarse scales after t i t_{i} . The earlier observation X 0 X_{0} therefore has more information about the fine scales at time t i t_{i} than the current observation X t i X_{t_{i}} and the distribution of X t i + 1 X_{t_{i+1}} given X t i X_{t_{i}} changes when we also condition on X 0 X_{0} . In other words, the observed process is not Markov. A cascade replaces the actual fine scales, at each of its S S stages, by a fresh draw from those compatible with the current observation. This loss of memory under coarse graining is classical in optimal prediction and in the Mori–Zwanzig formalism, where the history of the observed variables enters their reduced dynamics as a memory term ( Chorin et al., 2000 ; Chorin et al., 2002 ; Ma et al., 2019 ) . An exact transition maps the distribution of X t i X_{t_{i}} to that of X t i + 1 X_{t_{i+1}} , so a cascade of exact transitions, averaged over X 0 X_{0} , produces the correct distribution of the state at every time of the partition. What can be wrong is the dependence of the forecast on X 0 X_{0} (Appendix C.6 ). This cannot be detected by pooling statistics over initial conditions, such as energy spectra(Section 2 ). For smooth deterministic dynamics, a cascade of exact transitions converges, as the transitions shrink, to a deterministic flow driven by the conditional mean velocity of the observed state, whose error is at least the conditional standard deviation of the true forecast (Theorem C.10 ). To see why, consider the size of the terms. Over a transition of length δ \delta , the unobserved components push the observed state by an amount of order δ \delta . Along a true trajectory, these pushes persist and add up to a spread of order T T , whereas the cascade draws them anew at each stage, so that their fluctuations average out and only their mean survives.

sections.heading: Connection between analysis and experiment.
sections.text: This model shares two key features with the PDE experiments: the dependence of the forecast on the conditioning variable becomes more complicated as the horizon grows, and an unobserved component carries information across transitions. Its dynamics are linear in ( Y t , H t ) (Y_{t},H_{t}) for fixed c c , so its behavior requires neither nonlinearity nor chaos. It suggests three things: cascading helps when the forecast depends on the observation in a complicated way; very deep cascades lose accuracy when unobserved components act on the observed ones strongly and persistently, and the stronger they act, the shallower the best cascade; and cascading does not help when the direct forecast is simple, as at ω = 0 \omega=0 . In the next section we experimentally study how these two effects play out across five PDE systems.

sections.heading: The experimental dynamical systems.
sections.text: We select five physical systems to investigate conditional forecasting under different physical dynamics and forms of unobserved initial uncertainty (Figure 3 and Table 1 ). They comprise nonlinear fluid dynamics, wave propagation, and linear transport. In particular, we include both nonlinear and linear dynamics to investigate whether the benefits of cascading extend beyond systems with nonlinear interactions or chaotic sensitivity to initial conditions. Appendix B.1 gives the equations, initial distributions, numerical solvers, and convergence checks. Euler ( euler ). The vorticity of an inviscid fluid is transported by a velocity field that is determined by the vorticity itself. The resulting nonlinear interactions couple spatial scales, so the unobserved fine-scale vorticity influences the observed coarse evolution. Surface quasi-geostrophic flow ( sqg ). The surface buoyancy of a rapidly rotating, stratified fluid is transported in the same way ( Held et al., 1995 ) , but the velocity depends more strongly on fine-scale variations of the buoyancy than in Euler flow. The unobserved scales therefore have a stronger influence on the flow that transports the observed ones. Heterogeneous waves ( het-waves ). Damped linear waves propagate in a medium with a fixed, spatially varying wave speed, which scatters them. The state comprises the displacement and the velocity. The observed initial displacement consists of the coarse scales of randomly placed shapes on a random background; the unobserved fine-scale displacement is confined to the interiors of the shapes, so its distribution depends on the observation, and the unobserved initial velocity consists of three Gaussian kicks at random locations. The forecaster observes the coarse displacement and a velocity proxy computed from two consecutive displacement snapshots, which is zero at t = 0 t=0 . Nonlinear Klein–Gordon ( nonlinear-kg ). A scalar field undergoes dispersive wave propagation with a cubic restoring force. As in the wave system, the state comprises the field and its time derivative, but here the forecaster observes the coarse scales of both. The cubic term couples Fourier modes, so the fine scales influence the coarse ones through a local interaction instead of through transport. Passive scalar ( passive-scalar ). A scalar is advected by a steady cellular flow and diffuses. Its evolution is linear, and its unobserved fine scales are Gaussian and independent of the observation. The conditional distribution of the future is therefore Gaussian, with a mean that depends affinely on the observation and a covariance that does not depend on it (Proposition C.4 ). sections.heading: Forecasters.
sections.text: Direct SI learns a single conditional stochastic interpolant from X 0 X_{0} to X T X_{T} ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . It connects the two states by a stochastic path in an auxiliary time τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \tau\in[0,1] , learns the drift of this path by regression, and generates a forecast by integrating the resulting stochastic differential equation from X 0 X_{0} . Cascaded SI learns the transitions from X t i X_{t_{i}} to X t i + 1 X_{t_{i+1}} in the same way, with one network shared by all transitions and conditioned on their physical start and end times. EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , a strong diffusion-model baseline, is trained on the same endpoint pairs as Direct SI. For each system, all methods use the same U-Net, with channel widths 64 64 , 128 128 , and 256 256 and circular convolutions, acting on a 32 × 32 32\times 32 reconstruction of the observed modes. Hyperparameters, checkpoints, and the cascade depth S ⋆ ∈ { 1 , 2 , 5 , 10 , 20 , 40 } S^{\star}\in\{1,2,5,10,20,40\} are selected on the validation ensembles by the conditional energy distance ( Székely and Rizzo, 2013 ) , and the number of sampler steps is calibrated on validation data. The test ensembles are used only for the final evaluation (Appendix B.2 ).

sections.heading: A fixed number of training constraints.
sections.text: A single trajectory provides one endpoint pair for Direct SI or EDM, but S S transition pairs for a cascade of depth S S . To compare learning the forecast horizon directly with learning it through shorter transitions, we therefore fix the number of supervised pairs at B = 16,000 B=16{,}000 : Direct SI and EDM use one endpoint pair from each of the 200 trajectories of every training ensemble, and Cascaded SI at depth S S uses all S S transitions of 200 / S 200/S trajectories per ensemble. Every run uses 30,000 30{,}000 optimizer updates. A deeper cascade receives no additional pairs or updates, it is trained on fewer distinct trajectories, and its forecasts require S S sequential sampler integrations. We emphasize that this is a harsh constraint. In this way we equalize the number of training constraints but not the variety of the training data, whereas in reality the intermediate observations are often simply available. Our goal is to ensure that we focus on the tradeoff between approximation and Markovianity.

sections.text: For each test observation x 0 ( e ) x_{0}^{(e)} , we draw N = 10,000 N=10{,}000 samples from the forecaster and compare them with the N N reference samples of the simulator. Because a forecast can reproduce realistic local patterns at the wrong locations (Figure 2 ), we use spatial FID ( Nash et al., 2021 ) . Unlike the standard FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , the features of spatial FID are sensitive to the spatial layout of the images. We verify that this makes the metric more sensitive to spatial misalignment on our data: for example, it penalizes a simple flip of the Euler fields much more strongly than standard FID (Appendix B.4 ). We report its average over the ten test observations, which we call csFID-10k, with the standard error of the mean (SEM) over the test observations, for one training seed. For the two wave systems, the features are computed from the displacement (Appendices B.3 – B.4 ).

sections.heading: Cascading recovers the conditional distribution.
sections.text: The last row of Figure 2 shows the cascaded forecast for the same Euler observation as the other rows. The cascaded forecast correctly captures the spatial structure of the reference conditional mean and the regions of high and low standard deviation, which the direct forecasts fail to reproduce. The same holds for heterogeneous waves, whose direct forecasts are far too variable (Appendix B.5 ). Table 2 quantifies the improvement over all test observations. On Euler, Cascaded SI at the validation-selected depth S ⋆ = 10 S^{\star}=10 reduces csFID-10k by a factor of about 3.5 3.5 relative to both Direct SI and EDM, and it is better than both on each of the ten test observations. We make the following observations: 1. Cascading helps in all three nonlinear systems. The improvement on Euler extends to SQG and Klein–Gordon, by factors of 2.3 2.3 and 5.7 5.7 relative to the better direct forecaster. 2. Neither nonlinearity nor chaos is necessary for cascading to help. The heterogeneous-wave dynamics are linear and nonchaotic, and the conditional mean is affine in the observation, yet Cascaded SI reduces csFID-10k by more than a factor of three relative to both Direct SI and EDM. The rotation model of Section 3 is linear as well. 3. For the passive scalar, cascading is detrimental. Validation selects S ⋆ = 1 S^{\star}=1 , and every added stage increases the error, from 8.7 8.7 at S = 1 S=1 to 75 75 at S = 40 S=40 (Figure 4 ); EDM achieves the lowest score. This is what the rotation model does at ω = 0 \omega=0 : the direct forecast is simple, and a cascade has little to gain. The passive scalar is linear like the waves, so linearity alone does not decide the outcome. Its conditional covariance does not depend on the observation, whereas that of the waves does, through the masked fine scales; the contrast suggests that this dependence is what the direct forecasters cannot capture. Whether cascading is beneficial therefore cannot be explained simply by the underlying physical dynamics. The results point instead to the difficulty of learning the conditional forecast distribution over the full horizon, which depends on the dynamics, the observation, and the distribution of the unobserved scales.

sections.heading: The best depth is finite and > 1 >1 .
sections.text: Figure 4 shows the test error at each cascade depth S S , with the model, checkpoint, and sampler resolution selected on validation data separately for each depth. For the other four systems, the best test performance occurs at an intermediate depth: S = 5 S=5 for heterogeneous waves and SQG, S = 10 S=10 for Euler, and S = 20 S=20 for Klein–Gordon (for SQG, validation selects S ⋆ = 10 S^{\star}=10 ). Shorter transitions are thus not always better, and the preferred depth depends on the forecasting problem. Under the fixed budget of 16,000 16{,}000 supervised transitions and 30,000 30{,}000 optimizer updates, however, deeper cascades are also trained on fewer distinct trajectories, integrate their samplers more often, and compound learning errors, so the deterioration at large depths need not be caused by memory loss alone. Figure 4: Intermediate-depth cascades improve conditional forecasting in four of five systems. Test csFID-10k versus cascade depth S S (values in Table 6 ). S = 1 S=1 is Direct SI; outlined markers: validation-selected S ⋆ S^{\star} ; dashed lines: EDM; error bars: ± 1 \pm 1 SEM over the ten test observations. The optimal depths seem to agree with the theory. Among other differences, the fine scales drive the velocity more strongly in SQG than in Euler flow, and on SQG we indeed find that a shallower cascade is better, S = 5 S=5 against S = 10 S=10 ; the optimal gain is similarly smaller ( 2.3 2.3 against 3.5 3.5 ). In the rotation model, a stronger contribution of the hidden process also leads to a shallower optimum, although we have not measured the memory of the two systems. The wave system illustrates the relevance of how the intermediate states in the cascades are structured. Composing deterministic next-state regressors that use the displacement alone, but not the velocity, reduces the correlation with the reference conditional mean from 0.73 0.73 after one transition to 0.11 0.11 after five; including the velocity proxy, initialized at zero as in the benchmark, improves it from 0.65 0.65 to 0.87 0.87 (Table 4 in Appendix B.1.3 ).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied why generative forecasters can sample the wrong distribution of future states given coarse observations of a physical system, and when cascading transitions over shorter time intervals helps. In our experiments, cascaded SIs recovered conditional distributions when direct forecasters failed to do so, for both linear and nonlinear dynamics, but cascading was detrimental for a scalar passively advected and diffused by a prescribed flow. Our analytical model explains both effects by the trade-off between the approximation error of long transitions and the memory error of repeated conditioning on a coarse-grained state.

sections.heading: Open questions.
sections.text: Training the direct forecasters on one future for each of many observations, as in trajectory data, would show whether they fail because the forecast is irregular or because they see few distinct observations (Section 4 ). The experiments do not isolate memory loss as the cause of the deterioration at large depths (Section 5 ), but the reference ensembles make it possible to vary the other factors one at a time. The theory does not predict the depth selected in the PDE experiments; this will require substantial follow-up work, for example measuring how strongly and persistently the unobserved scales drive the observed ones. The analysis also suggests other remedies: conditioning every transition on the initial observation as well removes the memory error of exact transitions (Proposition C.11 ), and a cascade can carry a summary of the past, as the wave velocity proxy does. Finally, cascading increases inference cost, and its benefit may depend on model capacity.

sections.heading: Generative models for probabilistic forecasting.
sections.text: Recent work has used conditional diffusion models ( Batzolis et al., 2021 ; Baldassari et al., 2023 ) and stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) to represent distributions over future states rather than produce a single deterministic forecast. Chen et al. (2024) formulate forecasting directly as sampling from the conditional distribution of a future state given the current state, using stochastic interpolants to define a generative path between them. Related diffusion-based approaches have been developed for weather forecasting, including SEEDS ( Li et al., 2023 ) and GenCast ( Price et al., 2025 ) , and for complex physical systems and turbulent flows ( Kohl et al., 2026 ; Mücke and Sanderse, 2026 ) . Our work considers the same probabilistic forecasting objective, but focuses on how the physical time interval used for learning affects the accuracy of the resulting conditional distribution.

sections.heading: Using intermediate times and composing forecasts.
sections.text: Several forecasting methods make use of intermediate physical states or generate trajectories by repeatedly applying learned transitions. GenCast, for example, learns a conditional distribution over a fixed physical time step and samples successive states autoregressively ( Price et al., 2025 ) . Conditional diffusion models have similarly been applied autoregressively to turbulent-flow simulation ( Kohl et al., 2026 ) . Deterministic weather models have compared step lengths: Pangu-Weather composes models trained for several lead times so as to keep the number of steps small, since errors accumulate with every step ( Bi et al., 2023 ) , and Stormer averages forecasts made with different step lengths ( Nguyen et al., 2024 ) . For conditional diffusion models of PDEs, Shysheya et al. (2024) find that sampling a trajectory autoregressively forecasts better than sampling it all at once. DYffusion ( Rühling Cachay et al., 2023 ) is particularly related to our setting, since it uses intermediate physical times to build a dynamics-informed diffusion process. These works show that intermediate temporal information can be useful for forecasting, and they evaluate forecasts against single realized futures. We instead compare learning P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}) directly with learning and composing transitions over intervals of length T / S T/S , at a fixed final time T T and against reference ensembles of the conditional distribution. We vary S S while keeping the number of supervised training pairs fixed. This exposes a non-monotone dependence on cascade depth: making the transitions shorter can improve the forecast, but dividing the interval increasingly finely need not continue to help, and for a passive scalar every added stage makes the forecast worse.

sections.heading: Iterated and direct multi-step forecasts.
sections.text: In time-series analysis, the choice between iterating a one-step model and estimating a separate model for each horizon has long been studied ( Marcellino et al., 2006 ; Chevillon, 2007 ) . For linear autoregressions, it is a trade-off between estimation variance and bias: iterated forecasts are more efficient when the one-step model is correctly specified, while direct forecasts are more robust to misspecification. The two effects in our analysis play analogous roles: a transition over a short interval is easier to approximate than one over the full horizon, which is the approximation effect, and a one-step model of the observed process is misspecified whenever this process is not Markov, which is the memory effect. We study these effects for generative forecasts of the full conditional distribution of high-dimensional physical fields, made with models of limited capacity, rather than for point forecasts with linear models.

sections.heading: Partial observation and memory.
sections.text: The second effect in our analysis is specific to forecasting from incomplete observations. Projection of a dynamical system onto a subset of its variables generally produces dynamics with memory: unresolved variables can retain information about the past that is not contained in the current observation. This phenomenon is classical in optimal prediction and the Mori–Zwanzig formalism ( Chorin et al., 2000 ; Chorin et al., 2002 ) . It has a direct consequence for cascaded probabilistic forecasts. Even if each short transition P ⁡ ( X t i + 1 ∣ X t i ) P(X_{t_{i+1}}\mid X_{t_{i}}) were known exactly, their composition need not equal P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}) when the observed process is not Markov. Our theoretical analysis makes this loss of information explicit and studies its competition with the approximation error of learning longer transitions. In the rotation–OU model, these two effects produce a finite optimal cascade depth.

sections.heading: Evaluating conditional forecast distributions.
sections.text: Evaluating generative models is difficult because realistic individual samples do not by themselves imply that the correct distribution has been learned ( Theis et al., 2016 ) . Probabilistic forecasting methods therefore use ensemble-based scores, distributional statistics, and diagnostics of forecast uncertainty ( Li et al., 2023 ; Price et al., 2025 ; Kohl et al., 2026 ) . Our benchmark is designed specifically for conditional evaluation under partial observation. For each observed initial state x 0 x_{0} , we generate many full initial states that share x 0 x_{0} but differ in their hidden components, and evolve each of them with the physical simulator. The resulting reference ensemble gives direct samples from P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0}) . This allows us to distinguish a model that generates plausible states from one that recovers the conditional distribution associated with the particular observation supplied to the forecaster.

sections.heading: Appendix C How cascading changes forecast error
sections.text: A forecast over a fixed horizon T T can be learned directly, in a single transition, or through a cascade of shorter transitions. The experiments in the main text show that shorter transitions can substantially improve the conditional forecast, but that the improvement can stop as the cascade becomes deeper. In this section, we study two mechanisms that can produce this behavior. First, a fixed approximation class may represent a short transition well while failing to represent the dependence that develops over a longer interval. Composing several simple maps can then represent dependence that a single map in the same class cannot. Second, under partial observation, repeatedly conditioning only on the current observed state can discard information carried by the unresolved state. We study these two effects separately before combining them in the rotation model from the main text, in which a hidden Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process drives the dynamics. To keep the analysis explicit, we use forecast classes built from polynomial functions of the observed state. These provide a tractable setting in which we can calculate when the dependence of the forecast on its input leaves a fixed function class and how composing shorter fitted transitions changes the resulting error. We then study exact short conditional kernels to isolate the effect of repeated conditioning under partial observation. Finally, we analyze both effects together in the rotation–OU model, giving an example in which an intermediate cascade depth is optimal. The memory effect that appears under partial observation is classical in optimal prediction Chorin et al. (2002) ; Ma et al. (2019) .

sections.heading: C.6 What repeated conditioning in a cascade forgets
sections.text: Corollary C.9 shows that a cascade of shorter transitions can reduce approximation error when the full state is observed. We now return to the partially observed setting. Here cascading introduces a second effect: at the end of each stage, the next transition is conditioned only on the current observed state. Information carried by the unresolved variables, and by their relation to earlier observations, may therefore be lost. We first study this effect using exact short-transition distributions. There is therefore no learning error in the analysis below. Any difference between the direct conditional law and the cascade is caused only by repeated conditioning on the observed state.

sections.heading:
C.7 Direct and cascaded forecasts in the rotation–OU model:
an explicit trade-off
sections.text: The previous results identify two opposing effects of cascading. Shorter transitions can be easier to approximate, but repeated conditioning on the observed state can discard information carried by unresolved variables. Those general results do not yet show whether these effects can produce an optimal intermediate cascade depth. We now exhibit this behavior in a model for which the generated endpoint distribution can be calculated explicitly. This is the model introduced in Section 3 . We proceed in three steps. First, we construct a family of forecasting problems with the same target endpoint distribution but different amounts of hidden memory. Second, we compute the endpoint distribution generated by Direct SI and Cascaded SI for a specified quadratic learner. Finally, we compare direct forecasting, fine cascades, and an intermediate cascade.

Alexandra Spitzer Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Basel, Switzerland Giovanni Abati Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Basel, Switzerland Lorenzo Baldassari Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Basel, Switzerland Till Muser Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Basel, Switzerland Cheng Shi & Ivan Dokmanić Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Basel, Switzerland Affiliation: Département d’Informatique, École Normale Supérieure, PSL University, Paris, France Abstract We study probabilistic forecasting of dynamical systems such as fluids and waves from coarse observations. Since the unseen fine scales influence the dynamics, the same coarse initial state can evolve into a whole distribution of futures. Generative forecasters may produce visually plausible samples, but it is hard to tell whether they sample the right conditional distribution, since trajectory data contain a single future for each initial state. We address this problem by generating reference data in a hierarchical way: for each coarse initial state, we generate many different fine-scale components and numerically evolve the full states. Using these conditional ensembles, we show that standard diffusion models and stochastic interpolants make substantial distributional errors. We then show that cascading shorter forecasts greatly reduces these errors for the turbulent flows and waves we study, but we also find and characterize cases in which it hurts. Since the coarse process is not Markov, cascading discards information about the unresolved fine scales even with exact transitions. To understand this, we propose a solvable analytic model which shows that the optimal cascade depth decreases as the coupling between the unresolved and observed scales gets stronger, and increases as the dependence of the forecast on the observation becomes more oscillatory. Consistent with our experiments, cascading is detrimental when the direct forecast is “easy” to learn, for example Gaussian as in the passive scalar case. We release our datasets as a first benchmark for probabilistic forecasting with ground-truth conditional ensembles. 1 Introduction Suppose we observe a turbulent flow on a coarse grid and want to predict what it will look like some time later. The grid resolves the large scales, but the unobserved fine (subgrid) scales also influence the dynamics. In 1969, Lorenz argued that in a flow with many scales, a fine-scale error propagates to ever larger ones. Two states that differ only in smallest details become as different as two random states, in finite time ( Lorenz, 1969 ; Palmer et al., 2014 ) . Weather forecasting is a classic example of this “butterfly effect” ( Lorenz, 1963 ) . The same coarse observation X 0 X_{0} is therefore consistent with many futures X T X_{T} , one for each subgrid realization, and the forecast is the conditional distribution P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}) ( Chorin et al., 2000 ; Chorin et al., 2002 ) . A modern approach is to learn P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}) with conditional generative models such as diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021 ) and stochastic interpolants (SIs) ( Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ) 1 1 1 A more detailed discussion is in Appendix A . trained on pairs of initial and final observed states. These models generate samples of future weather and turbulent flows ( Price et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Kohl et al., 2026 ) which resemble real physical states, but do they actually sample from the right conditional distribution ( Theis et al., 2016 ) ? Testing this is a challenging problem. One reason is that the conditional distribution describes all futures consistent with a given observation but available data usually only contain one trajectory per initial state. Here we address this challenge. We design an experiment that lets us show that common generative forecasters can make substantial distributional mistakes. We then study a way to reduce these mistakes by better using the available data: forecasting over shorter time intervals and composing the results. Practical forecasters already do this, but mostly as a matter of convenience. Our goal is to understand when and why it helps, and when it can actually hurt. The experiment works as follows. For five spatio–temporal systems with different dynamical characteristics we first generate coarse states and then complete each coarse state with many independently drawn fine-scale components (Section 2 ). The full states are identical under coarse graining, but the dynamics (computed by a numerical solver) evolve them into different coarse futures. For each coarse initial state this yields a reference ensemble from the conditional distribution, whose statistical properties can be studied empirically. We test a standard conditional SI and a conditional diffusion model trained directly on initial–final pairs ( X 0 , X T ) (X_{0},X_{T}) , and find that they can be substantially wrong. Figure 2 shows an example for Euler flow (second and third rows). Their samples have visually correct local statistics, but the global structure is completely wrong. Diffusion models and SIs generate samples via stochastic dynamics in an auxiliary “diffusion” time. This dynamics is in general very different from the physical dynamics of the system over the forecasting period. A forecaster trained only on pairs ( X 0 , X T ) (X_{0},X_{T}) has to learn in one fell swoop everything the physical dynamics does between 0 0 and T T . But the physical dynamics is a composition of many short steps. As intermediate observations at times 0 < t < T 0<t<T are often available ( Rühling Cachay et al., 2023 ; Rozet and Louppe, 2023 ) , it is natural to ask whether they can be leveraged to improve conditional forecasting. Instead of learning P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}) directly, one can learn the conditional transitions P ⁡ ( X t i + 1 ∣ X t i ) P(X_{t_{i+1}}\mid X_{t_{i}}) over S S shorter intervals and compose them into a cascade of depth S S . In a cascade of SIs, the generative path is then forced to agree with the physical evolution at some intermediate times. In the Euler example, such a cascaded SI approach is much better than direct and it effectively reproduces the conditional distribution (last row of Figure 2 ). In practice, the depth of a cascade is set by a fixed time step: GenCast rolls out a twelve-hour transition over fifteen days ( Price et al., 2025 ) , and conditional diffusion models and SIs for fluid simulation use the time step of the training data ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Kohl et al., 2026 ; Mücke and Sanderse, 2026 ) . Cascading can, however, also discard information even with exact transitions. Only the full state evolves by composing short steps. After coarse graining, the unresolved fine scales carry information from one interval to the next, so that the coarse process is not Markov. To our knowledge, there is no analysis of how cascading affects the learned distribution. The questions we ask here are: is it better to forecast directly or with a cascade, what properties of the physical system determine the answer, and how deep should a cascade be? We propose a solvable model to answer these questions (Section 3 ). The optimal cascade depth results from the interplay between easier learning and memory loss, and depends on the specific system under study. If the conditional distribution is easy to learn over the full horizon, cascading can be detrimental. This is the case for a scalar field passively advected by a steady flow, whose conditional distribution stays Gaussian at every horizon, with a mean affine in the observation and a covariance that does not depend on it (Section 5 ). Our main contributions are the following. • An experimental design that enables proper evaluation of the conditional distribution. New datasets for five physical systems, with different simulated futures for each observed initial state, allow us to compare learned and true conditional distributions on every observation (Sections 2 and 4 ). To our knowledge, these are the first datasets designed for this notoriously challenging problem; we release them as an openly accessible benchmark. We find that diffusion models and SIs trained directly over the forecast horizon sample substantially wrong conditional distributions in four of the five systems, despite producing visually plausible samples. • A theoretical explanation. For smooth dynamics, we show that, through nonlinear interactions, the conditional mean leaves a fixed approximation class as the horizon grows, and that, under partial observation, a fine cascade of exact transitions loses the conditional spread of the forecast. We construct a stylized model of a rotating system driven by a hidden Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process where we compute the error of a simple SI exactly and prove that it is minimized at a finite depth S ⋆ ≥ 2 S^{\star}\geq 2 ; with the rotation switched off, every cascade is worse than the exact direct forecast (Section 3 ). • An experimental test. At a fixed number of supervised transitions, cascading reduces the error of the direct forecasters by factors between 2.3 2.3 and 5.7 5.7 , with the smallest error at an intermediate depth, for nonlinear flows and linear waves alike. For the passive scalar, every added stage increases the error, consistent with the analysis (Section 5 ). 2 Conditional forecasting from coarse observations We consider a physical system whose full state Y t Y_{t} evolves according to Y t = 𝒢 t ​ ( Y 0 ) Y_{t}=\mathcal{G}_{t}(Y_{0}) . A forecaster sees only the coarse state X t = ℋ ⁡ ( Y t ) X_{t}=\mathcal{H}(Y_{t}) . At the initial time, we write Y 0 = ( X 0 , Z 0 ) Y_{0}=(X_{0},Z_{0}) , where Z 0 Z_{0} contains the fine-scale components. Since the observation X 0 = x 0 X_{0}=x_{0} generally does not determine Z 0 Z_{0} , different full initial states consistent with the same observation can lead to different observed futures. The forecasting task is therefore to learn the conditional distribution P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0}) (2.1) for every observation x 0 x_{0} . In our systems, Y t Y_{t} consists of one or two fields on a two-dimensional periodic domain, simulated on grids ranging from 128 2 128^{2} to 1024 2 1024^{2} points. The observation map ℋ \mathcal{H} keeps only their Fourier modes with 0 < | k | ≤ 8 0<|k|\leq 8 (196 real coordinates per field), while the unresolved initial modes extend to higher wavenumbers that depend on the system (Appendix B.1 ). To measure its accuracy, we would like to compare the learned and the true conditional distributions for each observation, using some metric D D on probability distributions, and then average over observations, ℰ ⁡ ( P ^ ) = 𝔼 x 0 ∼ P ⁡ ( X 0 ) ​ [ D ⁡ ( P ⁡ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) , P ^ ​ ( X T ∣ X 0 = x 0 ) ) ] . \mathcal{E}(\widehat{P})=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}\sim P(X_{0})}\Bigl[D\bigl(P(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0}),\,\widehat{P}(X_{T}\mid X_{0}=x_{0})\bigr)\Bigr]. But data usually contain only one future per observed initial state, with all observed states being different. Proper scoring rules can rank forecasters on such data ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) , but they cannot determine how far they are from the true conditional. Averaging final spectra or other statistics over initial conditions only tests the marginal distribution P ⁡ ( X T ) P(X_{T}) . Comparing the joint distributions of ( X 0 , X T ) (X_{0},X_{T}) could in principle work because they determine the conditionals. The issue is that a forecaster that generates the “correct” forecast for a slightly perturbed observation would have a nearly correct joint distribution, but the forecasts could be completely wrong if they are sensitive to the initial state (which is often the interesting regime). Hierarchical data generation. When the system can be simulated, this problem can be addressed by sampling the initial data hierarchically. For each conditioning ensemble e e , we first sample the coarse scales x 0 ( e ) ∼ P ⁡ ( X 0 ) x_{0}^{(e)}\sim P(X_{0}) , and then many different fine scales for this coarse state, z 0 ( e , i ) ∼ P ( Z 0 ∣ X 0 = x 0 ( e ) ) , Y 0 ( e , i ) = ( x 0 ( e ) , z 0 ( e , i ) ) , i = 1 , … , n . z_{0}^{(e,i)}\sim P\bigl(Z_{0}\mid X_{0}=x_{0}^{(e)}\bigr),\qquad Y_{0}^{(e,i)}=\bigl(x_{0}^{(e)},z_{0}^{(e,i)}\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n. Connection between analysis and experiment. This model shares two key features with the PDE experiments: the dependence of the forecast on the conditioning variable becomes more complicated as the horizon grows, and an unobserved component carries information across transitions. Its dynamics are linear in ( Y t , H t ) (Y_{t},H_{t}) for fixed c c , so its behavior requires neither nonlinearity nor chaos. It suggests three things: cascading helps when the forecast depends on the observation in a complicated way; very deep cascades lose accuracy when unobserved components act on the observed ones strongly and persistently, and the stronger they act, the shallower the best cascade; and cascading does not help when the direct forecast is simple, as at ω = 0 \omega=0 . In the next section we experimentally study how these two effects play out across five PDE systems. 4 Experimental design The experimental dynamical systems. We select five physical systems to investigate conditional forecasting under different physical dynamics and forms of unobserved initial uncertainty (Figure 3 and Table 1 ). They comprise nonlinear fluid dynamics, wave propagation, and linear transport. In particular, we include both nonlinear and linear dynamics to investigate whether the benefits of cascading extend beyond systems with nonlinear interactions or chaotic sensitivity to initial conditions. Appendix B.1 gives the equations, initial distributions, numerical solvers, and convergence checks. Euler ( euler ). The vorticity of an inviscid fluid is transported by a velocity field that is determined by the vorticity itself. The resulting nonlinear interactions couple spatial scales, so the unobserved fine-scale vorticity influences the observed coarse evolution. Surface quasi-geostrophic flow ( sqg ). The surface buoyancy of a rapidly rotating, stratified fluid is transported in the same way ( Held et al., 1995 ) , but the velocity depends more strongly on fine-scale variations of the buoyancy than in Euler flow. The unobserved scales therefore have a stronger influence on the flow that transports the observed ones. Heterogeneous waves ( het-waves ). Damped linear waves propagate in a medium with a fixed, spatially varying wave speed, which scatters them. The state comprises the displacement and the velocity. The observed initial displacement consists of the coarse scales of randomly placed shapes on a random background; the unobserved fine-scale displacement is confined to the interiors of the shapes, so its distribution depends on the observation, and the unobserved initial velocity consists of three Gaussian kicks at random locations. The forecaster observes the coarse displacement and a velocity proxy computed from two consecutive displacement snapshots, which is zero at t = 0 t=0 . Nonlinear Klein–Gordon ( nonlinear-kg ). A scalar field undergoes dispersive wave propagation with a cubic restoring force. As in the wave system, the state comprises the field and its time derivative, but here the forecaster observes the coarse scales of both. The cubic term couples Fourier modes, so the fine scales influence the coarse ones through a local interaction instead of through transport. Passive scalar ( passive-scalar ). A scalar is advected by a steady cellular flow and diffuses. Its evolution is linear, and its unobserved fine scales are Gaussian and independent of the observation. The conditional distribution of the future is therefore Gaussian, with a mean that depends affinely on the observation and a covariance that does not depend on it (Proposition C.4 ).
